note: Drafted by the chat assistant 11-04 for the owner's review (D150 T03b, first wider-CS batch). Nothing is live until approved in Admin → Learn → Questions. 'pieces' are suggested Learn step ids to verify.

items.stem: A function that should return a customer's last three orders sometimes returns only two. You can reproduce it with one customer's data. What do you do first?
choices: Rewrite the function from scratch
Write a failing test that reproduces it with that data, fix the bug, and keep the test
Ask a teammate to look at it
Add print statements throughout the codebase
why: You may rewrite the same bug, and you won't know when it's actually fixed.
A failing test pins the bug down, proves the fix works, and stops it coming back.
Asking is fine later, but you already have what you need to find it.
Scattered prints are slow and get left behind; a focused test is faster.

items.stem: You committed to main by mistake and haven't pushed yet. Your team works on feature branches. How do you fix it?
choices: Delete the repository and clone it again
Push it anyway and mention it in chat
Create a branch at your current commit, then reset main back to match origin/main
Force-push main later once the feature is done
why: You'd lose the work, or have to redo it.
Main now has unreviewed work that everyone pulls.
Your commit moves to its own branch and main goes back to where the team expects it, with nothing lost.
Force-pushing a shared branch rewrites history under your teammates.

items.stem: You need to check whether any two numbers in a list of one million add up to a target. Your nested loops are far too slow. What do you use instead?
choices: Recursion over every pair
The same nested loops, split across more threads
A hash set of the numbers seen so far: for each number, check whether target minus it is already in the set
Sort the list, then keep the nested loops
why: Still every pair, plus call overhead.
Still around a trillion comparisons, just in parallel.
One pass with constant-time lookups turns quadratic work into linear.
Sorting doesn't help if you still compare every pair.

items.stem: Your pull request touches 30 files and 2,000 lines, and reviewers keep approving it without real comments. What should you do?
choices: Merge it late on a Friday when traffic is low
Ask for more reviewers on the same pull request
Merge it, since it's approved
Split it into small pull requests that each do one thing, behind a feature flag if needed, each with its tests
why: Friday merges mean nobody is around if it breaks.
More people skimming 2,000 lines doesn't make it reviewed.
An approval nobody could meaningfully give isn't a review.
Small changes get real review, are easier to roll back, and can ship safely in pieces.

items.stem: A test fails about one run in twenty in CI, and the team has started re-running builds until they pass. What do you do?
choices: Add an automatic retry until the test passes
Ignore it; it passes most of the time
Delete the test
Quarantine it with an owner, find the cause (usually timing, ordering or shared state), and fix it
why: Retries hide real bugs that also show up intermittently in production.
Teams soon learn to ignore every failure.
You lose the coverage it gave you.
Quarantining stops it blocking everyone, and fixing the cause (a fake clock, isolated data, an awaited call) makes CI trustworthy again.

items.stem: Ten minutes after your release, error rates double. You're not sure why. What do you do first?
choices: Push a quick fix based on your best guess
Wait to see whether it settles down
Roll back (or turn off the feature flag), then investigate with the logs and the diff
Restart the servers until errors drop
why: A guess under pressure can make it worse.
Users are hitting errors while you wait.
Restoring service comes first, and rolling back is the fastest known-good state. Then you investigate calmly.
Restarts rarely fix a code change, and they hide the evidence.

items.stem: A page renders a table of 10,000 rows, and scrolling is laggy. What's the fix?
choices: Add a longer debounce to scrolling
Render it all on the server instead
Memoise every row component
Virtualise the list so only the rows on screen are rendered
why: Doesn't reduce the work; scrolling just feels delayed.
Faster first paint, but the browser still handles 10,000 rows.
Fewer re-renders, but you still have 10,000 rows in the page.
Rendering only what's visible keeps the page light no matter how long the list is.

items.stem: Content jumps around as images load, and users tap the wrong button. What stops it?
choices: Hide the page until all images have loaded
Give every image its width and height (or an aspect ratio) so its space is reserved before it loads
Lazy-load more of the images
Compress the images
why: Users wait longer, and the shift happens anyway on slow images.
The browser lays out the page correctly from the start, so nothing moves when images arrive.
Loading later doesn't reserve space; the jump still happens.
Smaller files load sooner, but the layout still shifts.

items.stem: A clickable <div> works with a mouse, but keyboard and screen-reader users can't use it. What's the right fix?
choices: Add an aria-label to the div
Add an onKeyDown handler to the div
Use a real <button> element
Add tabindex="0" to the div
why: A label without the role and keyboard support doesn't make it usable.
Part of it, but it's still not announced as a button and misses some keys.
A button is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced correctly, all built in.
It can be focused, but still doesn't act like a button.

items.stem: Your JavaScript bundle has grown to 3 MB, and first load on mobile is slow. What do you do?
choices: Serve it from a CDN
Minify it harder
Preload everything so it's cached
Analyse the bundle, split code by route, lazy-load heavy libraries, and remove unused code
why: Faster delivery of the same 3 MB still has to be parsed and run.
It's probably minified already; the size is in what's included.
Preloading makes the first load heavier.
Users then download only what the first screen needs, and the rest arrives when it's used.

items.stem: The same server data lives in several stores and keeps getting out of sync, and props are passed down six levels. What's the better structure?
choices: Sync every store through localStorage
One server-state cache (a query library) as the single source of truth for server data, with UI state kept close to where it's used
Put everything in one global store
Copy the data into each component that needs it
why: Adds a slow, string-based copy on top of the existing ones.
Server data gets one cached source with refetching built in, and local state stays local, so the copies disappear.
A single big store still mixes server and UI state and grows hard to reason about.
More copies, more drift.

items.stem: User profile bios are rendered with innerHTML. What's the risk, and what's the fix?
choices: Cross-site scripting: render bios as plain text, or sanitise with an allow-list, and add a Content Security Policy
Strip <script> tags with a regular expression
None, since users are logged in
Escape only < and >
why: Rendering as text, or allowing only safe markup, stops injected code, and a CSP limits the damage if something slips through.
Script can run without a <script> tag (onerror, javascript: links).
Logged-in users can still attack each other.
Attributes and event handlers like onerror still get through.

items.stem: Your app keeps login tokens in localStorage. What's the safer approach?
choices: Keep the session in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, with CSRF protection
Use sessionStorage instead
Put the token in the URL
Encrypt the token before putting it in localStorage
why: Scripts can't read an httpOnly cookie, so an XSS bug can't steal the session, and SameSite plus CSRF tokens block cross-site requests.
Same exposure to scripts as localStorage.
URLs leak through history, logs and referrers.
Any script on the page can still read and send it.

items.stem: An infinite feed uses offset pagination. As new posts arrive, users see duplicates and miss items. What do you change?
choices: Switch to cursor (keyset) pagination: fetch items after the last one seen
Use a larger page size
Show posts in random order
Remove duplicates on the client
why: A cursor anchors each page to a real item, so new posts don't shift what comes next.
Fewer pages, same shifting problem.
Users lose any sense of the feed.
Hides duplicates but still misses items.

items.stem: Users upload large videos through your API servers, and uploads time out. What's the better design?
choices: Raise the request timeout
Have the client upload straight to storage with a pre-signed URL, then process the file in the background
Use bigger API servers
Send the file as base64 inside JSON
why: Long uploads still hold connections open and fail on bad networks.
Uploads go directly to storage built for it, your servers stay free, and processing happens asynchronously.
Costs more and the upload still passes through your servers.
Makes files a third larger and loads them into memory.

items.stem: You're shipping a risky change to checkout. How do you release it?
choices: Keep it on a long-lived branch until it's perfect
Release to everyone and watch the dashboards
Release to everyone at once, late on Friday
Behind a feature flag, rolled out gradually (internal, then 1%, then more) while watching the key metrics, with a kill switch
why: Long-lived branches drift and become a big-bang merge.
Everyone is exposed before you know if it works.
If it breaks, it breaks for everyone, with nobody around.
A small first audience limits the damage, metrics tell you when to continue, and the switch undoes it instantly.

items.stem: Search runs LIKE '%term%' over five million rows and takes seconds. What do you do?
choices: Limit results to ten
Add a regular index on the column
Cache every query
Use full-text search: the database's full-text index or a search engine
why: The database still scans every row to find them.
A normal index can't help a pattern with a leading wildcard.
Most searches are different; the cache rarely hits.
Full-text indexes are built for word search: fast, ranked, and they handle word forms.

items.stem: A payment provider's webhooks sometimes arrive twice and out of order. How do you handle them?
choices: Process each one immediately, in the order received
Verify the signature, record each event id so a repeat is ignored, apply events by their timestamp or version, and acknowledge quickly before processing in a queue
Stop using webhooks and poll the API every minute
Ignore anything that arrives within five seconds of the last one
why: Duplicates double-apply and out-of-order events overwrite newer state.
Signatures stop forged events, ids make repeats harmless, ordering by version keeps state right, and a queue keeps responses fast.
Slower, costlier, and you still need the same care with ordering.
Drops real events and still lets duplicates through.

items.stem: Every deploy causes a short outage. What removes it?
choices: Use bigger instances
Deploy at night
Rolling or blue-green deploys with readiness checks, so traffic only reaches instances that are ready
Restart the servers by hand after each deploy
why: Size doesn't change how traffic switches over.
Fewer people notice, but it's still an outage.
New instances take traffic only once they're healthy, and old ones drain first, so users never hit a gap.
Manual steps add risk and still drop requests.

items.stem: Your database server ran out of disk at 3 a.m. What should have prevented it?
choices: A nightly restart
Alerts on the growth trend (for example, full within 7 days), log rotation, and capacity planning
Deleting old files by hand when space runs low
A bigger disk, added when it filled up
why: Restarts don't free disk.
Alerting on the trend gives you days to act during working hours, and rotation and planning stop it recurring.
Relies on someone noticing in time.
Reactive, and it happened at 3 a.m. anyway.

items.stem: You find a production database password committed in the repository's history. What do you do?
choices: Rotate the password now, remove it from history, move secrets to a secret manager, and add secret scanning before commits
Delete the file in the next commit
Make the repository private
Encode the password in base64
why: Rotation makes the leaked password useless, the manager keeps secrets out of code, and scanning stops the next one.
It's still in history for anyone to read.
Everyone who already had access still has it.
Base64 isn't encryption; anyone can decode it.

items.stem: On-call gets 200 alerts a week, and most need no action. What do you change?
choices: Page only on user-facing symptoms (for example, SLO burn rate), and send the rest to tickets or dashboards
Page the whole team so someone responds
Add more alerts so nothing is missed
Mute the noisy alerts
why: Pages then mean users are affected, so people trust and act on them.
Everyone gets tired, and responsibility gets diluted.
More noise means real alerts get ignored.
Quieter, but real problems can hide in the muted set.

items.stem: Pods keep being killed for running out of memory under load. What's the right approach?
choices: Set requests and limits from measured usage, fix any memory leak, and autoscale on the metric that actually tracks load
Move to bigger nodes and change nothing else
Set the restart policy to always
Remove the memory limits
why: Right-sized limits protect the node, fixing the leak removes the cause, and the right autoscaling metric adds capacity before memory runs out.
Hides a leak until the bigger node fills too.
They already restart; that's the symptom, not a fix.
One pod can then starve others on the same node.

items.stem: A two-hour outage is resolved. What happens next?
choices: Find out who caused it
Nothing, since it's fixed
A blameless postmortem: a timeline, the contributing factors, and a few action items with owners and dates
Write a long report and file it
why: Blame makes people hide information next time.
The same failure will come back.
Focusing on how the system allowed it produces fixes people actually complete.
A report nobody acts on changes nothing.
